name: Scout
description: The Scout rank is the first step: learning the ideals of Scouting, how a troop and patrol work, a few foundational skills, and personal safety. It is usually completed soon after joining.

provenance.notes: Topic outline drafted from maintainer familiarity with the Scouts BSA rank requirements (the structure introduced in 2016 and revised since) and cross-referenced with secondary sources found by web search. Official rank requirements could not be reached from the build environment.

references.label: Wikipedia: Ranks in Scouts BSA (secondary source)

requirements.title: Scouting ideals
requirements.summary: The Scout Oath, Scout Law, motto, slogan, Outdoor Code and Pledge of Allegiance, and the signs and symbols of Scouting.

children.title: Oath, Law, motto, and slogan
children.summary: Reciting the Scout Oath, Scout Law, motto and slogan from memory and explaining what they mean to you.

children.title: Scout spirit
children.summary: What Scout spirit means and examples of how you have shown it.

children.title: Sign, salute, and handshake
children.summary: Demonstrating the Scout sign, salute and handshake and when each is used.

children.title: The First Class badge
children.summary: Describing the First Class Scout badge and what its parts stand for.

children.title: The Outdoor Code
children.summary: Reciting the Outdoor Code and explaining what it means to you.

children.title: The Pledge of Allegiance
children.summary: Reciting the Pledge of Allegiance and explaining its meaning.

requirements.title: How a troop works
requirements.summary: After attending a troop meeting: how youth lead the troop, the steps of advancement, the ranks, and how merit badges are earned.

children.title: Youth leadership
children.summary: How Scouts in the troop provide its leadership.

children.title: Steps of advancement
children.summary: The steps a Scout goes through to advance.
children.orientation: Advancement follows a predictable cycle: you learn a skill, you are tested on it, you are reviewed, and you are recognized. Knowing the cycle helps you understand why sign-offs, conferences and boards of review exist — and why a personal checklist like this one is never the same as an official sign-off.

children.title: The ranks
children.summary: What the Scouts BSA ranks are and how they are earned.

children.title: Merit badges
children.summary: What merit badges are and how they are earned.

requirements.title: The patrol method
requirements.summary: How the patrol method works and getting to know your own patrol.

children.title: Patrol method
children.summary: Explaining the patrol method and the types of patrols in a troop.

children.title: Your patrol
children.summary: Learning your patrol’s name, emblem, flag and yell, and why patrol identity matters.

requirements.title: Rope skills
requirements.summary: Tying basic knots and caring for rope.

children.title: Three basic knots
children.summary: Tying a square knot, two half hitches and a taut-line hitch, and explaining how each is used.
children.orientation: Each of these knots has a job. The square knot joins two ends of the same material, such as a bandage. Two half hitches tie a line to a post or ring. The taut-line hitch makes an adjustable loop, which is why it is used on tent guylines. Learn the job first and the knot is easier to remember. Animated step-by-step guides help, but tie each one with real rope until you can do it without looking.

children.title: Rope care
children.summary: Whipping and fusing rope ends to keep them from unraveling.

requirements.title: Pocketknife safety
requirements.summary: Showing that you know how to handle a pocketknife safely.

requirements.title: Personal safety
requirements.summary: Personal-safety exercises completed with a parent or guardian.
requirements.note: This requirement has changed in recent years (older versions referred to the Cyber Chip and a parent’s guide to child-abuse prevention; newer materials refer to personal safety awareness training). Use the current official wording.
